# Color templates for consistency

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, dpi = 150)
library(hvtiPlotR)
library(ggplot2)
```

hvtiPlotR plots carry no colour scale by default. ggplot2's [@R-ggplot2]
`scale_colour_*` controls
line and point colours; `scale_fill_*` controls filled areas (ribbons, bars).
Both take the same `name` (legend title) and `guide` (legend display)
arguments. Set them together so the two scales stay in sync.

## When to use it

Colour is the fastest way to separate groups on a figure, and the easiest to
overuse. Reach for a manual colour scale when the groups have a convention you
want to honour (a brand colour, red for the high-risk arm) or when you have one
series and want it off the default grey. Reach for a ColorBrewer palette
when the groups are arbitrary and you want a set of hues that stay distinct in
print and for colour-blind readers. Reach for a journal palette when a
co-author wants the figure to look like the target journal's own. And reach for legend suppression whenever
the figure already names its groups some other way, since a colour that needs no
key earns back panel space.

The guiding question is what the colour is *for*. If it carries information, the
distinct group it marks, it has to survive a black-and-white printer and a
colour-blind reader, which is where palette choice and a second visual channel
come in. If it is decoration, keep it to one or two restrained hues. We use a
grouped trends plot below so the colour mapping is visible across levels.

```{r}
#| label: base
dta_trends <- sample_trends_data(n = 600, seed = 42)
p_base     <- plot(hv_trends(dta_trends))
```

## Manual colours

Use `scale_colour_manual()` / `scale_fill_manual()` to assign specific brand or
convention colours to known levels. Here a single-stratum KM curve is set to one
colour.

```{r}
#| label: fig-colors-manual
#| fig-cap: >-
#|   Single-stratum survival curve with a manual color scale assigning one named
#|   color to the lone level. A solid steel-blue step line traces survival and a
#|   pale steel-blue band its confidence interval.
dta_km <- sample_survival_data(n = 500, seed = 42)
km     <- hv_survival(dta_km)

plot(km) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(All = "steelblue"), guide = "none") +
  scale_fill_manual(values  = c(All = "steelblue"), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 100, 20),
                     labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 20, 5)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 20), ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(x = "Years after Operation", y = "Freedom from Death (%)") +
  theme_hv_manuscript(base_size = 12)
```

## Choosing a palette

Every figure in this book uses a colour-blind-safe palette, and so should
yours. About one man in twelve has some red-green colour deficiency, which is
enough that a reviewer, a co-author or a conference audience will include one.
The house rule has three parts.

- **Categorical groups** take the house palette, `hv_palette()`: the
  Okabe-Ito hues, ordered for a white background. It returns the same six
  colours as `hv_ppt_palette("light")` under a name that does not tie a
  manuscript figure to slides, and the
  [next section](#the-house-slide-palette) explains the order.
- **Ordered or diverging scales** take ColorBrewer's `"RdBu"` or `"PuOr"`, and
  **sequential** scales take `"Blues"`, through `scale_fill_brewer()`.
- **Avoid `"Set1"` and `"RdYlGn"`.** Both put red against green, the one
  contrast colour blindness most often erases.

Colour is still not enough on its own, because none of these palettes survive a
greyscale printer. Pair it with a second channel, point shape or line type, as
the figure below does.

```{r}
#| label: fig-colors
#| fig-cap: >-
#|   Grouped trends plot colored by the color-blind-safe house palette, with a
#|   matched point shape per group. Smooth lines and points are blue squares
#|   (Group I), vermillion circles (Group II), green triangles (Group III) and
#|   reddish purple diamonds (Group IV).
p_base +
  scale_colour_manual(values = hv_palette(), name = "Group") +
  scale_shape_manual(
    values = c("Group I" = 15, "Group II" = 19,
               "Group III" = 17, "Group IV" = 18),
    name = "Group"
  ) +
  labs(x = "Surgery Year", y = "Outcome") +
  theme_hv_manuscript(base_size = 12)
```

## The house slide palette

`hv_ppt_palette()` hands back the six colours `hv_ppt_series()` assigns across a
deck, as a plain character vector. Reach for it when a figure needs those
colours outside the decorator, so the script uses the one definition instead of
hex codes pasted out of an older script, which go stale the first time the
palette changes.

```{r}
#| label: ppt-palette
hv_ppt_palette("dark")
hv_ppt_palette("light", n = 4)
```

These are Okabe-Ito colourblind-safe hues, with one exception in the light
ordering (below), reordered for the background the figure will sit on. The high-luminance ones lead on a dark slide, where yellow
sits at more than 15:1 against a black panel, and the darker ones lead on a
light slide. So the first two or three series, the ones a figure most often
needs, separate hardest from the surface behind them.

Read that as a tendency, not a guarantee. The orderings are not strictly sorted
by contrast. Black is the clearest case: it appears only in the light ordering,
where it has the strongest contrast of the six against white by a wide margin,
and it is nonetheless held back to sixth. Keeping it out of the leading
positions is worth it, because a black series on a light panel reads as axis ink
rather than as data, which is the same reason annotation takes black there. They
are not CORR brand colours either, and nothing stops a project from handing its
own set to `scale_colour_manual()` instead.

Contrast is a separate question from order. WCAG 2.2 asks for 3:1 against the
background for any chart mark a viewer needs to read the data [@WCAG22:2023],
and as of hvtiPlotR 2.8.3 every color in the light ordering clears it on white.

| Position | Color | Hex | Contrast on white |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Blue | `#0072B2` | 5.19:1 |
| 2 | Vermilion | `#D55E00` | 3.87:1 |
| 3 | Bluish green | `#009E73` | 3.42:1 |
| 4 | Reddish purple | `#CC79A7` | 3.06:1 |
| 5 | Darkened yellow | `#9D952B` | 3.10:1 |
| 6 | Black | `#000000` | 21:1 |

: Contrast on white of `hv_ppt_palette("light")` as of hvtiPlotR 2.8.3, in palette order, computed with the WCAG relative-luminance formula. {#tbl-colors-ppt-light-contrast}

The fifth color is the one departure from stock Okabe-Ito: their yellow,
darkened at the same hue to `#9D952B`. Orange used to sit there at 2.25:1, and
orange darkened far enough to reach 3:1 came out too close to vermilion under a
deuteranopia simulation. The guarantee assumes a white slide.
`theme_hv_ppt_light()` leaves the figure background transparent, so it holds on
the white house template and not on a tinted one. The dark ordering is
unchanged and clears 3:1 on the black panel of `theme_hv_ppt_dark()`. Why
contrast matters on a projected slide, and how the stock Okabe-Ito set fares on
white, is in [designing slides](slide_design.qmd).

Six colours are the entire supply, which covers a grouping variable up to six
levels. Ask for a seventh and you get an error rather than a quietly recycled
palette, on the reasoning that two series sharing a colour is worse than a
stopped script.

Pair the `"light"` ordering with `theme_hv_manuscript()` and a journal figure
takes the same hues the deck does, so one analysis looks like itself in both
places.

```{r}
#| label: fig-colors-ppt-palette
#| fig-cap: >-
#|   Grouped trends plot taking the light-background ordering of the house
#|   palette, with the matching point shapes. Smooth lines and points are blue
#|   circles (Group I), vermillion triangles (Group II), green squares (Group
#|   III) and reddish purple diamonds (Group IV).
p_base +
  scale_colour_manual(values = hv_ppt_palette("light")) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 17, 15, 18)) +
  labs(x = "Surgery Year", y = "Outcome") +
  theme_hv_manuscript(base_size = 12)
```

The shape scale is not decoration here. Okabe-Ito is built to survive colour
blindness, which is not the same thing as surviving a greyscale printer, so the
second channel still has work to do. And the colours are only half the recipe.
The deck-wide decorator that assigns them, and the theme that rides along with
them, are in [slides and presentations](presentations.qmd).

## Journal palettes

Sooner or later a co-author asks for a figure "in the NEJM colours". The
`ggsci` package [@R-ggsci] packages those looks: each palette is a list of hues
taken from figures a journal has published, wrapped as a pair of ggplot2 scales.
Eight of its palettes are journals.

| Journal | Colour scale | Fill scale | Colours |
|---|---|---|---|
| New England Journal of Medicine | `scale_colour_nejm()` | `scale_fill_nejm()` | 8 |
| The Lancet | `scale_colour_lancet()` | `scale_fill_lancet()` | 9 |
| JAMA | `scale_colour_jama()` | `scale_fill_jama()` | 7 |
| BMJ | `scale_colour_bmj()` | `scale_fill_bmj()` | 9 |
| Journal of Clinical Oncology | `scale_colour_jco()` | `scale_fill_jco()` | 10 |
| Science (AAAS) | `scale_colour_aaas()` | `scale_fill_aaas()` | 10 |
| Nature (NPG) | `scale_colour_npg()` | `scale_fill_npg()` | 10 |
| Frontiers | `scale_colour_frontiers()` | `scale_fill_frontiers()` | 10 |

: Journal palettes in `ggsci`, with the number of colours each holds. {#tbl-colors-journal}

The rest of the package's palettes are not journals (genome browsers, web
frameworks, television), and none of the cardiothoracic journals we publish in
most, *JTCVS*, *The Annals of Thoracic Surgery* or *EJCTS*, has one. For those
the house palette stays the default.

A journal scale drops in exactly where the house palette went. Keep the shape
scale, for the reason the next paragraphs give.

```{r}
#| label: fig-colors-journal
#| fig-cap: >-
#|   Grouped trends plot colored by the NEJM palette from ggsci, with a matched
#|   point shape per group. Smooth lines and points are red squares (Group I),
#|   blue circles (Group II), orange triangles (Group III) and green diamonds
#|   (Group IV).
library(ggsci)

p_base +
  scale_colour_nejm(name = "Group") +
  scale_shape_manual(
    values = c("Group I" = 15, "Group II" = 19,
               "Group III" = 17, "Group IV" = 18),
    name = "Group"
  ) +
  labs(x = "Surgery Year", y = "Outcome") +
  theme_hv_manuscript(base_size = 12)
```

When you need the colours themselves, for an annotation or a table cell, each
scale has a `pal_*()` twin. `pal_nejm()(4)` returns the first four NEJM hex
codes, in the order the scale assigns them. They carry an eighth and ninth
digit, `FF`, which is the opacity, and ggplot2 takes them as they are.
@fig-colors-journal-swatches lays the journal palettes side by side in that
order.

```{r}
#| label: fig-colors-journal-swatches
#| fig-cap: >-
#|   The eight journal palettes in ggsci, in the order each scale assigns colors
#|   to groups. Each row is one journal and each tile one palette position,
#|   numbered along the x axis and filled with that position's color.
swatch <- function(journal, pal, n) {
  data.frame(journal = journal, position = seq_len(n), hex = pal()(n))
}
swatches <- rbind(
  swatch("NEJM", pal_nejm, 8),   swatch("Lancet", pal_lancet, 9),
  swatch("JAMA", pal_jama, 7),   swatch("BMJ", pal_bmj, 9),
  swatch("JCO", pal_jco, 10),    swatch("AAAS", pal_aaas, 10),
  swatch("NPG", pal_npg, 10),    swatch("Frontiers", pal_frontiers, 10)
)
swatches$journal <- factor(swatches$journal, levels = rev(unique(swatches$journal)))

ggplot(swatches, aes(position, journal, fill = hex)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
  labs(x = "Position in palette", y = NULL) +
  theme_hv_manuscript(base_size = 12)
```

None of this relaxes the rule from [choosing a palette](#choosing-a-palette).
These palettes were picked to match a journal's look, not to survive colour
blindness, and they differ a good deal. We ran the first four colours of each,
the ones a two-to-four group figure uses, through `colorspace`'s simulations of
the two red-green deficiencies. Lancet puts its red second and its green third,
the exact pairing the house rule bans. BMJ's first and fourth colours, a blue and
a purple, become almost the same colour under deuteranopia, and AAAS's navy and
purple come close. Frontiers opens with red, orange, yellow and green, a run of
neighbouring hues that crowd together under either deficiency. JAMA, JCO and NPG held up about as well as the house palette,
and NEJM nearly so. So a journal palette is a choice to check, not one to trust,
and the shape channel stays on either way.

Last, a journal look is not a journal requirement. What author guidelines ask of
a figure is usually resolution, file format and legibility rather than
particular hues, and some journals redraw accepted figures in their own style
regardless. Read the target journal's figure instructions before choosing a
palette on looks.

## Suppressing legends

Pass `guide = "none"` to any scale and that aesthetic drops out of the legend.
Do this when axis labels or an annotation already name the group, so a redundant
legend does not eat panel space.

```{r}
#| label: fig-colors-no-legend
#| fig-cap: >-
#|   The grouped plot with both color and shape legends suppressed with guide set
#|   to none, relying on redundant color and shape channels. Smooth lines and
#|   points are blue squares (Group I), vermillion circles (Group II), green
#|   triangles (Group III) and reddish purple diamonds (Group IV).
p_base +
  scale_colour_manual(values = hv_palette(), guide = "none") +
  scale_shape_manual(
    values = c("Group I" = 15, "Group II" = 19,
               "Group III" = 17, "Group IV" = 18),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  labs(x = "Surgery Year", y = "Outcome") +
  theme_hv_manuscript(base_size = 12)
```

@fig-colors-no-legend pairs colour with a distinct point shape per
group. That redundancy is deliberate, and it is the heart of the first pitfall
below.

## Pitfalls

- **Colour as the only channel.** If the only thing separating two groups is
  their hue, the figure fails for a sizeable fraction of readers (red-green
  colour blindness alone affects roughly one man in twelve) and for anyone who
  prints it in greyscale, where two mid-tone colours collapse to the same grey.
  The fix is cheap: give each group a second channel as well, a point shape or a
  line type, so the distinction survives even when the colour does not. The
  recipes here map `scale_shape_manual()` alongside the colour scale for exactly
  this reason. A quick check is to convert the figure to greyscale and confirm
  you can still tell the groups apart.
- **Too many hues.** A palette with eight saturated colours does not help a
  reader; it asks them to memorise a legend and hunt for matches. Past about
  four or five groups, distinct colours stop being distinct and the figure turns
  to confetti. When you have many series, consider showing fewer at once,
  faceting into small panels, or muting the background series in grey and
  colouring only the one or two you are making a point about.
- **Running a journal palette past its length.** Each `ggsci` palette is a
  fixed list (@tbl-colors-journal). Give the seven-colour JAMA scale an eighth
  group and it warns, then leaves that group with no colour at all. Unlike
  `hv_ppt_palette()`, it does not stop the script, so the warning is the only
  sign. Check the group count against the palette before you trust the figure.
